twist.stem: On a fasting day, Sana eats no dal, eggs or grains. Which snack on her plate still brings some protein?
twist.hint: Think beyond dal, eggs and grains.

options.text: A bowl of sweet potato chaat.
options.feedback: Sweet potato is a root, not one of the protein foods. Nuts and seeds carry a good amount of protein.

options.text: Roasted peanuts and pumpkin seeds.
options.feedback: Yes. Nuts and seeds hold a good amount of protein, so they help on a day without dal or eggs.

options.text: A plate of fruit, since fasts allow no protein.
options.feedback: A fast can still hold protein. Nuts and seeds carry a good amount, while fruit is not a protein food.

transfer.stem: Gita runs a kirana shop in a Bihar village. A customer who eats no meat or eggs asks for protein-rich food. Which shelf fits?
transfer.hint: Think of the plant and dairy foods on the list.

options.text: Rice, atta and poha, since grains fill you up.
options.feedback: Grains fill the stomach, but the rich protein foods are milk, eggs, fish, meat and pulses, plus nuts and seeds.

options.text: Bunches of palak and methi.
options.feedback: Leafy greens are not on the protein list. Dal, milk and nuts are the plant and dairy picks for protein.

options.text: Dal, milk, peanuts and roasted chana.
options.feedback: Right. Pulses and milk are rich in protein and nuts carry a good amount, so no meat or eggs are needed.

twist.stem: Idli batter is rice and urad dal ground together. Mani eats plain idli with coconut chutney. Does the idli fill both building-block gaps?
twist.hint: Look at what goes into the batter.

options.text: No; grinding them up undoes the pairing.
options.feedback: Grinding them together does not undo the pairing. The cereal and the pulse still bring what the other is low in.

options.text: No; it needs an egg on the side to fill a gap.
options.feedback: An egg brings all nine blocks, but it is not the only fix. A cereal with a pulse also covers the gaps.

options.text: Yes; the rice and dal in it cover each other.
options.feedback: Yes. Idli holds a cereal and a pulse, so each brings plenty of the block the other is low in.

transfer.stem: A farmer in Rajasthan grows bajra and moong to feed his family. Why is that pair a good fit for protein?
transfer.hint: Sort the two crops into their food groups.

options.text: Any two crops fill gaps, so the pair does not matter.
options.feedback: Two cereals share the same low block. It is the millet and pulse pair that covers each other's gap.

options.text: Millet and pulse fill each other's gap.
options.feedback: Right. Bajra is a millet and moong is a pulse, so each brings plenty of what the other runs short of.

options.text: Bajra by itself carries plenty of each block.
options.feedback: Cereals and millets run low in one block. Moong, a pulse, brings plenty of it, which is why the pair helps.

twist.stem: Asha is a healthy adult, and her daily protein need comes out at about 54 g. About how much does she weigh?
twist.hint: Work back from the per-kg number.

options.text: About 54 kg, at one gram per kilo.
options.feedback: The figure is 0.83 g per kg, not 1 g. At that rate, 54 g fits a weight of about 65 kg.

options.text: About 27 kg, at two grams per kilo.
options.feedback: Two grams per kilo is far above the healthy adult figure of 0.83 g. At 0.83 g, 54 g fits about 65 kg.

options.text: About 65 kg, using the per-kg figure.
options.feedback: Yes. At 0.83 g for each kg, a 65 kg adult needs about 54 g a day.

transfer.stem: Tenzin, 60 kg, trains hard each day for his state kabaddi team in Sikkim. His plan uses the healthy adult figure per kg. What is off?
transfer.hint: Check who the per-kg number is set for.

options.text: Athletes may need more.
options.feedback: Right. The 0.83 g figure is for healthy adults in general. People who train hard may need more.

options.text: Nothing; the per-kg figure fits each adult alike.
options.feedback: The figure fits healthy adults in general. Teens, pregnant women and athletes may need more than it gives.

options.text: He may need less, since training saves protein.
options.feedback: Training does not lower the need. Athletes may need more protein than the healthy adult figure, not less.

twist.stem: Gajar halwa is made from carrots, milk and added sugar. Which of its sugars go in the free-sugar count?
twist.hint: Split it by where each part came from.

options.text: The carrot and milk sugar as well.
options.feedback: Sugar inside vegetables and plain milk is left out of the count. Only the sugar stirred in counts.

options.text: Just the sugar stirred in.
options.feedback: Yes. Added sugar counts as free sugar, while the sugar inside carrots and milk is left out.

options.text: None of it, since it is made at home.
options.feedback: Home cooking does not change the count. Sugar added in any kitchen is free sugar.

transfer.stem: For a cricket team's drinks break in Pune, the manager can serve whole oranges, orange squash, or 100% orange juice. Which adds no free sugar?
transfer.hint: Juice and syrup count, even when they come from fruit.

options.text: The 100% juice, since no sugar was added.
options.feedback: Fruit juice counts as free sugar even with nothing added. Only the sugar inside whole fruit is left out.

options.text: The orange squash, since it is made from fruit.
options.feedback: Squash is a syrup with sugar in it, so it counts. Coming from fruit does not take it off the list.

options.text: The whole oranges, cut into slices.
options.feedback: Right. Sugar inside whole fresh fruit is left out of the count, while juice and squash both count.

twist.stem: A kheer recipe lists 25 g of added sugar in one bowl. How much of the day's free-sugar limit is one bowl?
twist.hint: Compare 25 g with the 50 g mark.

options.text: About a quarter of it.
options.feedback: The limit is about 50 g, so 25 g is half of it, not a quarter.

options.text: About half of the day's limit.
options.feedback: Yes. The day's limit is about 50 g, or 12 teaspoons, so 25 g is about half.

options.text: More than the whole day's limit.
options.feedback: The limit is about 50 g, so 25 g fits under it. It uses about half.

transfer.stem: On Holi, Ritu has thandai with 4 teaspoons of sugar, three laddoos with 2 teaspoons each, and chai with 2 teaspoons. Where does her day land?
transfer.hint: Add them up and compare with the daily mark.

options.text: About at the limit of 12 teaspoons.
options.feedback: Right. 4 plus 6 plus 2 makes 12 teaspoons, which is about the 50 g mark. Less may bring more benefit.

options.text: Well under it, since festival sweets made at home do not count.
options.feedback: Sugar added at home still counts as free sugar. Her 12 teaspoons reach about the day's limit.

options.text: Far past it; the limit is about 3 teaspoons.
options.feedback: The limit is about 12 teaspoons, or 50 g. Her 12 teaspoons sit at about that mark.

twist.stem: Prakash eats no sweets but adds three spoons of ketchup to his fries. About how much free sugar is that?
twist.hint: Recall what one spoon of ketchup holds.

options.text: About 12 g, near three teaspoons.
options.feedback: Yes. One spoon of ketchup holds about 4 g, so three spoons bring about 12 g of free sugar.

options.text: None; ketchup is a salty sauce.
options.feedback: Ketchup tastes salty but holds about 4 g of free sugar per spoon. Sauces can hide sugar.

options.text: About 40 g, as much as a can of soda.
options.feedback: A can of soda can hold up to 40 g. Three spoons of ketchup bring about 12 g.

transfer.stem: At a Gurugram call centre, night staff get two free cans of soda each shift. How much of a 50 g daily limit can those two cans use?
transfer.hint: Double what one can may hold.

options.text: About a fifth of it, since drinks are light.
options.feedback: One can may hold up to 40 g, so two cans can hold up to 80 g. That is past the limit.

options.text: They can go past the whole limit.
options.feedback: Right. Each can may hold up to 40 g, so two can bring up to 80 g, more than 50 g.

options.text: About half of it.
options.feedback: Half would be 25 g. Two cans can hold up to 80 g, which is past the whole 50 g limit.

twist.stem: Lalitha drinks four glasses of water, 2 cups of coffee with little sugar and 2 glasses of milk. How close is she to the eight-glass mark?
twist.hint: Ask which drinks add fluid.

options.text: Halfway; water is the one drink that counts.
options.feedback: Milk and lower-sugar coffee count towards fluid too, so her day comes to about eight.

options.text: Short, since coffee takes water away.
options.feedback: Lower-sugar coffee counts towards daily fluid. With milk and water, she is close to eight glasses.

options.text: At the mark, since coffee and milk count.
options.feedback: Yes. Water, milk and lower-sugar coffee all add fluid, so her eight drinks reach the mark.

transfer.stem: During a week of exam study at home, Rohan barely moves. He thinks his body needs almost no fluid. What fits best?
transfer.hint: Think about how the body loses fluid.

options.text: Pee and sweat still take water out each day.
options.feedback: Right. Water leaves through pee and sweat even on a still day, so he still needs about 2 litres back.

options.text: Sport and hard work are what use up water.
options.feedback: Exercise adds sweat, but pee and sweat take water out all day, even while he sits and studies.

options.text: The body stores water, so one still week is fine.
options.feedback: Water leaves the body every day through pee and sweat, so it needs about 2 litres back each day.

twist.stem: By 4 pm at her shop, Usha feels tired and has peed only once since morning, but she is not thirsty. What fits best?
twist.hint: One cue is not the whole list.

options.text: She may be fine, since she is not thirsty.
options.feedback: Thirst is one cue among several. Tiredness and peeing less can also mean the body is short of water.

options.text: She may be low on fluid, thirst or not.
options.feedback: Yes. Tiredness and peeing less often are cues of low fluid, so she may need to drink more.

options.text: Tiredness is not a fluid cue.
options.feedback: Tiredness is one of the cues of low fluid, along with peeing less, a dry mouth and thirst.

transfer.stem: Pooja, a bank clerk in Patna, drinks often through the day, and her pee is clear pale yellow. A coworker thinks pale pee means something is wrong. What fits best?
transfer.hint: Pale yellow is the aim.

options.text: It means she drinks too little.
options.feedback: It is the other way. Dark yellow pee is the cue for too little fluid, while pale yellow is the aim.

options.text: Pee colour is not linked to fluid.
options.feedback: Colour is a simple cue. Pale yellow usually means enough fluid, and dark yellow means drink more.

options.text: It is a sign she drinks enough.
options.feedback: Right. Clear pale yellow pee is what most people can aim for, so her colour is a good sign.

twist.stem: On a very hot day, Gauri sits at a desk in a room with no fan and sweats all day. She does no exercise. Does her fluid need rise?
twist.hint: What makes the body lose water?

options.text: No; it takes exercise to raise the need.
options.feedback: Heat alone makes the body sweat, and sweat takes water out, so her need rises without any sport.

options.text: No; eight glasses covers any day, hot or cool.
options.feedback: Eight glasses is a rough guide. Heat and sweat take more water out, so the need goes up.

options.text: Yes; heat and sweat raise it on their own.
options.feedback: Yes. Sweat takes water out, so very hot weather raises the need even on a day with no exercise.

transfer.stem: At a long Ganpati procession in the sun, Omkar's cousin turns confused and cannot stand without dizziness, even after a drink. What fits best?
transfer.hint: Some signs need more than a drink.

options.text: Cool him in the shade, with a drink.
options.feedback: Shade and a drink help with heat, but confusion and dizziness that stays are red flags that call for urgent help.

options.text: Get urgent help now.
options.feedback: Right. Confusion or dizziness that does not pass can be signs of serious dehydration, so urgent help comes first.

options.text: Give him buttermilk and let him rest.
options.feedback: Buttermilk suits hot days, but confusion and dizziness that will not pass call for urgent help, not just rest.

twist.stem: Nitin usually sleeps 7 hours but stays up one hour later to watch a match. What may happen the next day?
twist.hint: Even a small cut can count.

options.text: Likely no change; one hour is too small.
options.feedback: Cutting sleep by even one hour can make it hard to focus the next day.

options.text: His body may repair less, but focus is fine.
options.feedback: Short nights cost both. Losing even one hour of sleep can make it harder to focus.

options.text: He may find it harder to focus.
options.feedback: Yes. Cutting sleep by even one hour can make it hard to focus, since sleep supports the brain.

transfer.stem: Arjun spends the evening learning a new tabla piece. Why does a full night's sleep after practice help?
transfer.hint: Think about what the brain does at night.

options.text: Practice is stored while awake, not in sleep.
options.feedback: Sleep is when the brain stores the day's learning, so the night after practice matters too.

options.text: Sleep just rests his tired hands.
options.feedback: Sleep repairs the body, but it also helps the brain store what he learned that day.

options.text: Sleep helps store the day's learning.
options.feedback: Right. Sleep helps the brain turn the day's learning into long-term memory, and that includes a new piece.

twist.stem: Gopal remembers a vivid dream from just before his alarm. Which sleep was he most likely in?
twist.hint: Which stage is the dreaming one?

options.text: Deep sleep, which fills the end of the night.
options.feedback: Deep sleep fills the early night. Vivid dreams come in REM sleep, which grows near morning.

options.text: REM sleep, which grows longer near morning.
options.feedback: Yes. REM is the dreaming stage, and it gets longer towards morning, just before the alarm.

options.text: Light sleep; dreams come as you drift off.
options.feedback: Most vivid dreams happen in REM sleep, which gets longer towards morning.

transfer.stem: After a long day of farm work in Bihar, Ramu sleeps from 10 pm to 5 am. In which hours does his body do the most repair?
transfer.hint: Think of when the deepest rest comes.

options.text: The early hours of his sleep, near bedtime.
options.feedback: Right. Deep sleep fills the early night, and the body does most of its repair in those hours.

options.text: The last hours, close to 5 am.
options.feedback: Deep sleep gets shorter towards morning, while REM grows. The early hours do most of the repair.

options.text: Evenly spread through the seven hours of sleep.
options.feedback: Sleep is not even. Deep sleep comes first in the night, so the early hours do most repair.

twist.stem: Tara wants to be asleep by 10 pm. By about what time would her phone go away?
twist.hint: Count back from bedtime.

options.text: At 9:59 pm, just before bed.
options.feedback: Screens are best off at least half an hour before bed, so about half past nine, not a minute before.

options.text: Any time, as long as the screen is dim.
options.feedback: The habit is screens off at least half an hour before bed, so about half past nine for a 10 pm bedtime.

options.text: By half past nine, or a bit before.
options.feedback: Yes. Screens off at least half an hour before bed means about half past nine for a 10 pm bedtime.

transfer.stem: Vinod works late shifts at a Bengaluru office and goes to bed at 10 pm. About what is the latest time for his last coffee?
transfer.hint: Count back the hours coffee can last.

options.text: Around 2 pm.
options.feedback: Right. Caffeine can take 8 hours or more to wear off, so 2 pm is about the latest for a 10 pm bedtime.

options.text: Around 8 pm.
options.feedback: Coffee at 8 pm could still be acting until 4 am, since caffeine can last 8 hours or more.

options.text: Any time; coffee wears off within an hour.
options.feedback: Caffeine can take 8 hours or more to wear off, so a late coffee can still act at bedtime.

twist.stem: Deepa walks briskly for 40 minutes, five days a week. Where does her week land?
twist.hint: Add up her week, then compare.

options.text: Inside the weekly range of 150 to 300.
options.feedback: Yes. 40 times 5 is 200 minutes, which sits inside the weekly range of 150 to 300.

options.text: Short; the aim is at least 300 minutes.
options.feedback: The range runs from 150 to 300 minutes. Her 200 minutes sit inside it.

options.text: Past the top; 150 is the most to do.
options.feedback: 150 is the low end of the range, not the top. Her 200 minutes sit inside 150 to 300.

transfer.stem: Gopal, a postman in a hill town, walks briskly on his round for 50 minutes, six days a week. His son thinks work walking does not count. What fits?
transfer.hint: Brisk is brisk, wherever it happens.

options.text: It counts, but it is still under 150 minutes.
options.feedback: 50 times 6 is 300 minutes, the top of the range, so it is well over 150.

options.text: It counts, and it reaches 300 minutes.
options.feedback: Right. A brisk walk raises heart rate and breathing at work too, and 50 times 6 is 300 minutes.

options.text: It does not count, since it is part of his job.
options.feedback: Brisk walking raises heart rate and breathing wherever it happens, so his round counts.

twist.stem: On an easy cycle ride, Rekha sings her favourite song with ease. What effort level is that?
twist.hint: Recall what the talk test checks.

options.text: Moderate, since she is moving the whole time.
options.feedback: Moderate effort lets you talk but not sing. If she sings with ease, she is below moderate.

options.text: Hard, since her legs keep turning the pedals.
options.feedback: Vigorous effort leaves room for only a few words. Singing with ease means a light effort.

options.text: Below moderate, since she can still sing.
options.feedback: Yes. Moderate effort stops you singing, so singing with ease means she is below that level.

transfer.stem: A dance teacher in Kolkata wants her class at a vigorous effort for one song. Which check fits?
transfer.hint: Recall the talk test for hard effort.

options.text: Dancers can chat but not sing.
options.feedback: Talk but not sing is the sign of moderate effort. Vigorous leaves room for only a few words.

options.text: Only a few words fit between breaths.
options.feedback: Right. Vigorous effort leaves room for only a few words before a breath, so that is her check.

options.text: Dancers are sweating through their clothes.
options.feedback: Sweat depends on heat too. The talk test is the gauge: vigorous leaves room for only a few words.

twist.stem: Shreya jogs 75 minutes a week and does no other activity. What part of the weekly plan is missing?
twist.hint: The plan has two parts.

options.text: None; her 75 hard minutes cover the plan.
options.feedback: Her jogging matches 150 moderate minutes, but the plan also needs muscle work on 2 days.

options.text: Muscle work on 2 days a week.
options.feedback: Yes. Her 75 jog minutes match 150 moderate ones, but adults also need muscle work on 2 days.

options.text: More jogging, to reach 150 minutes.
options.feedback: Vigorous minutes count double, so her 75 already match 150 moderate. Muscle work is what is missing.

transfer.stem: In an office step challenge in Hyderabad, Rina runs hard for 45 minutes twice a week. Her colleague walks briskly for 150 minutes. Whose minutes reach the weekly aim?
transfer.hint: Count each running minute twice.

options.text: The walker; Rina has just 90 minutes.
options.feedback: Vigorous minutes count double, so Rina's 90 match 180 moderate minutes, past the aim.

options.text: Rina, since running beats walking.
options.feedback: The walker's 150 moderate minutes reach the aim too. Brisk walking counts.

options.text: Both reach it, Rina by counting double.
options.feedback: Right. Rina's 90 vigorous minutes count as 180 moderate, and the walker has 150, so both reach it.

twist.stem: In a mixed office team in Chennai, which colleagues are more at risk of low iron?
twist.hint: Think of blood that leaves the body.

options.text: Those who sit at desks the whole day.
options.feedback: Desk work is not the link. Women with periods lose blood each month, so they are more at risk.

options.text: Women who have periods.
options.feedback: Yes. Periods take blood out of the body each month, so women who have them need more iron.

options.text: Nobody; men and women need the same iron.
options.feedback: Women who have periods lose blood each month, so they need more iron than men.

transfer.stem: A water tanker service in Chennai has fewer tankers than usual, so homes get less water. Which body chain works like this?
transfer.hint: Think of what does the carrying.

options.text: Less haemoglobin, so more oxygen is left for the legs.
options.feedback: Haemoglobin carries the oxygen. With less of it, less oxygen reaches the body, not more.

options.text: Less haemoglobin, but faster breathing fully makes up for it.
options.feedback: Breathing harder does not replace the carrier. With less haemoglobin, less oxygen arrives, which is why people feel tired.

options.text: Less haemoglobin, so less oxygen gets to the legs and arms.
options.feedback: Right. Like a tanker for water, it is the carrier. With fewer carriers, less oxygen gets to the body.

twist.stem: Three lunches of palak dal and roti differ only in the side. Which one lets the body take in the most iron?
twist.hint: Look for the helper and the blocker.

options.text: Palak dal with lemon, and tea an hour later.
options.feedback: Yes. Lemon's vitamin C helps plant iron in, and keeping tea away from the meal stops it holding iron back.

options.text: Palak dal with a cup of tea alongside it.
options.feedback: Tea holds back iron from plant foods, so drinking it with the meal lets less iron in.

options.text: Palak dal alone, since greens give plenty of iron.
options.feedback: Iron from greens is harder to take in. A vitamin C side like lemon helps more of it in.

transfer.stem: A wedding caterer in Lucknow serves chole and roti with masala chai poured during the meal. Which swap helps guests take in the most iron?
transfer.hint: One change adds a helper; one removes a blocker.

options.text: Serve more chai, since warm drinks help digestion.
options.feedback: Tea holds back iron from plant foods, so more chai with the meal lets less iron in.

options.text: Add lemon to the chole and serve chai later.
options.feedback: Right. Vitamin C in lemon helps plant iron in, and moving the chai an hour away stops it blocking.

options.text: Add a sweet, since sugar helps iron in.
options.feedback: Sugar is not the helper. Vitamin C foods like lemon help, and tea is best kept away from meals.

twist.stem: Anu eats plenty of iron-rich food, yet a test shows she has anaemia. What fits best?
twist.hint: Low iron is one of several.

options.text: Another cause may be behind it.
options.feedback: Yes. Anaemia has many causes, so a good diet does not rule it out. A test finds which one.

options.text: She may just need more spinach.
options.feedback: Low iron is one cause, but not the only one. Low B12 or thalassaemia can cause anaemia too.

options.text: The test may be wrong, since her diet is good.
options.feedback: Low iron is one cause, but not the only one. Low B12 or malaria can cause it too.

transfer.stem: In an Odisha village where malaria is common, a health worker finds many people low in haemoglobin. Will iron tablets alone fix them all?
transfer.hint: Check the flow of reasons again.

options.text: Yes, if they also eat more greens.
options.feedback: Greens add iron. But if malaria is the cause, iron alone will not fix it.

options.text: Yes; low blood iron is the one cause.
options.feedback: Anaemia has many causes. Malaria is one, so a test is needed to find each person's cause.

options.text: No; malaria is one more cause.
options.feedback: Right. Malaria is one cause of anaemia, so each person needs a test to find the cause before treatment.

twist.stem: A biscuit brand cuts its serving from 30 g to 20 g, and the sugar per serving drops. Did the biscuit get less sugary?
twist.hint: Who chose the new serving size?

options.text: Not by that; check the per 100 g line.
options.feedback: Yes. The brand sets the serving size, so a smaller serving lowers the number without changing the food.

options.text: Yes; less sugar per serving means a less sugary biscuit.
options.feedback: A smaller serving shows less sugar even if the recipe is the same. The per 100 g line shows the truth.

options.text: Yes, since brands must cut sugar to cut servings.
options.feedback: Brands pick serving sizes freely. Only the per 100 g line shows whether the recipe changed.

transfer.stem: A Kolkata gym trainer compares protein bars. Bar A has 12 g protein in a 48 g bar. Bar B has 14 g in a 70 g bar. Which has more protein per 100 g?
transfer.hint: Put both on the per 100 g line.

options.text: Bar B, since 14 g is more than 12 g.
options.feedback: Bar B is bigger. Per 100 g, Bar B has 20 g of protein and Bar A has 25 g.

options.text: They are equal, since each is one bar.
options.feedback: The bars weigh different amounts. Per 100 g, Bar A has 25 g and Bar B has 20 g.

options.text: Bar A, which has 25 g per 100 g.
options.feedback: Right. 12 g in 48 g is 25 g per 100 g, while 14 g in 70 g is 20 g per 100 g.

twist.stem: A masala oats pack lists: oats, maida, sugar, salt, spices. Is there more maida than sugar in it?
twist.hint: Earlier on the list means more.

options.text: No; the list order shows quality, not amount.
options.feedback: The order is by amount, most first. Maida comes before sugar, so there is more maida.

options.text: Yes, since maida comes before sugar.
options.feedback: Yes. Ingredients are listed from most to least, so maida, listed second, outweighs sugar, listed third.

options.text: You cannot tell from the list alone.
options.feedback: You can. The list runs from the largest amount to the smallest, so maida outweighs sugar.

transfer.stem: At a Hyderabad store, a 'honey almond' cereal lists: wheat flakes, sugar, honey, almonds 2%. What is it mostly made of?
transfer.hint: Read the list, not the name.

options.text: Honey and almonds, just as the name shows.
options.feedback: The name is a sales line. The list puts wheat flakes and sugar first, so they make up most of it.

options.text: Almonds, since nuts are weighed last.
options.feedback: The list runs from most to least, so almonds at the end are the smallest part, only 2%.

options.text: Wheat flakes, with sugar next in line.
options.feedback: Right. Ingredients run from most to least, so wheat flakes and sugar make up most of the cereal.

twist.stem: A bottle shows a big orange and the words 'real fruit drink'. The back lists water, sugar, then orange juice 8%. What is it mostly?
twist.hint: The front sells; the back tells.

options.text: Water and sugar, then a little juice.
options.feedback: Yes. A 'real fruit' drink can hold 10% fruit or less, and here water and sugar come first on the list.

options.text: Orange juice, just as the picture shows.
options.feedback: Pictures and front words sell the pack. The back lists just 8% juice, after water and sugar.

options.text: Equal parts juice and water.
options.feedback: The back shows 8% juice. A 'real fruit' drink can hold 10% fruit or less.

transfer.stem: In a Jaipur chemist shop, a face cream has 'with real aloe' in big letters on the front. What fits the label idea best?
transfer.hint: Which side of a pack sells?

options.text: It may be mostly aloe, since the front names it.
options.feedback: Front words are there to sell. Like 'real fruit' on a drink, the named item may be a small part.

options.text: Check the back list for the aloe.
options.feedback: Right. Front claims sell, and a 'real fruit' drink can hold 10% fruit or less, so the back list shows how much aloe.

options.text: Front claims usually name the main item.
options.feedback: A 'real fruit' drink can hold 10% fruit or less, so front claims do not show the main item.

twist.stem: Asif eats about 200 g of fruit and vegetables a day. Does that meet the daily aim?
twist.hint: Recall the grams on the card.

options.text: No; it is half the daily aim.
options.feedback: Yes. The aim is at least 400 g of fruit and vegetables a day, so 200 g is half of it.

options.text: Yes; any fruit counts as enough.
options.feedback: Some is better than none, but the aim is at least 400 g a day, so 200 g is half.

options.text: Yes; the aim is about 200 g.
options.feedback: The aim is at least 400 g a day, twice what Asif eats.

transfer.stem: A hostel mess in Guwahati serves rice and potato curry every day. Which change fits the idea that no single food has it all?
transfer.hint: Think of the food groups.

options.text: Add pulses, eggs or milk, and more fruit.
options.feedback: Right. Mixing food groups covers what rice and potato lack, since no one food has every nutrient.

options.text: No change; rice is filling, so it covers needs.
options.feedback: Feeling full is not the same as getting every nutrient. A mix of food groups does that.

options.text: Add a second cereal like roti.
options.feedback: Roti is another cereal. Pulses, milk or eggs, and fruit and vegetables add what cereals lack.

twist.stem: Before a dance show in Kolkata, Riddhi plans two no-food days to feel light on stage. What might happen on show day?
twist.hint: Recall what no-food days can bring.

options.text: She may feel weak, faint or get a headache.
options.feedback: Yes. No-food days can bring headaches, weakness and fainting, which is a risk on a show day.

options.text: She may have more energy from a light body.
options.feedback: Going without food tends to bring weakness, not energy. Headaches and fainting are known risks.

options.text: She may be fine, as long as she drinks juice.
options.feedback: Eating so little can still bring headaches, weakness and fainting, juice or not.

transfer.stem: An aunt in Kerala forwards a message: 'Detox water is proven to burn fat.' What fits best?
transfer.hint: Ask what makes the scale drop at first.

options.text: There is no strong proof that detox works.
options.feedback: Right. There is no strong proof that detox plans help weight loss. Early drops come from eating very little.

options.text: It is proven, since so many people share it.
options.feedback: Many shares are not proof. There is no strong research that detox plans help weight loss.

options.text: It works if it is drunk before sunrise.
options.feedback: Timing does not change it. There is no strong proof that detox plans help weight loss at all.

twist.stem: An app promises 4 kg off in 4 weeks. How does that compare with the pace called safe?
twist.hint: Half a kilo times four weeks.

options.text: About right; a kilo a week is slow.
options.feedback: The safe pace is about half a kilo a week. A kilo a week is double that.

options.text: About double the safe pace.
options.feedback: Yes. At half a kilo a week, 4 weeks gives about 2 kg. The app promises twice that.

options.text: Safe, since it lasts a whole month.
options.feedback: The length is not the test; the pace is. Half a kilo a week gives about 2 kg in 4 weeks, not 4.

transfer.stem: An office in Hyderabad plans a prize for whoever loses the most weight in two weeks. Why is that a poor design?
transfer.hint: Think about which pace wins the prize.

options.text: It is fine, since faster loss lasts longer.
options.feedback: Very fast loss often does not last and can miss nutrients. Slow loss is the safer pace.

options.text: It rewards the fastest loss.
options.feedback: Right. Very fast loss often does not last and can miss nutrients. About half a kilo a week is called safe.

options.text: It is fine if people also drink detox tea.
options.feedback: Detox tea does not make fast loss safe. Slow loss of about half a kilo a week is the safe pace.
